title: India By Era
coverage: Selected milestones from 1947 to January 2026. This is a curated history, not a complete record of events through October 2026.

eras.title: The Foundation & Nation-Building Era
eras.question: How do you turn independence into a republic?
eras.intro: Freedom brought both possibility and catastrophe. India had to accommodate displaced families, integrate princely states and create institutions for a vast democracy. Under Jawaharlal Nehru, public investment and planning became central to economic policy.
eras.tension: Political equality arrived before economic equality. A common citizenship had to coexist with deep differences of language, caste, religion and income.
events: Independence, and the trauma of Partition
British rule ended on 15 August. Partition created India and Pakistan and triggered mass displacement and communal violence.
Freedom and forced migration belonged to the same moment. Rehabilitation and the protection of minorities became urgent tasks for the new state.
Bringing the princely states into the Union
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and V. P. Menon helped bring more than 500 princely states into India through accession and integration.
The process was not uniform. Junagadh, Hyderabad and Jammu and Kashmir followed different, contested paths. Territorial integration also continued beyond 1950.
Nathuram Vinayak Godse assassinated Mahatma Gandhi at Birla House in Delhi on 30 January 1948, less than six months after independence.

The killing belongs within the history of the early republic, alongside constitution-making and state integration. Independence had not ended political violence or the struggle over communal coexistence.
The Election Commission of India was established on 25 January 1950, immediately before India became a republic. Its constitutional role provided the institutional basis for organising elections.

Universal adult franchise needed an administrative system as well as a constitutional promise. The Commission’s establishment in 1950 and the first general election in 1951–1952 were separate steps. Assessments of particular elections require their own evidence.
The Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949. Most provisions came into force on 26 January 1950, when India became a republic.

The Constitution established parliamentary government, fundamental rights and a federal structure. Its original Preamble described a Sovereign Democratic Republic. The words Socialist and Secular were added in 1976.
Planning begins with farms and irrigation
The First Five-Year Plan prioritised agriculture, irrigation and recovery after Partition. Planning aimed to direct scarce capital towards development.
The Second Plan, beginning in 1956, put greater emphasis on heavy industry and the public sector. Agriculture and industry were successive priorities, not a single policy launched in 1951.
The first IIT is formally inaugurated

IIT Kharagpur was formally inaugurated by Education Minister Maulana Abul Kalam Azad on 18 August 1951. It became the first institute in the IIT system, following planning that began before independence.

Technical education formed part of the effort to build industrial and scientific capacity. The inauguration was one milestone in an institutional process, rather than the beginning of every kind of engineering education in India.
India held its first general election under universal adult franchise in 1951–1952. Congress won, and Nehru continued as prime minister.
A competitive election made constitutional democracy a working practice. The initial voting age was 21. It was lowered to 18 through the 61st Amendment in 1988.
A law against the practice of untouchability

Parliament enacted the Untouchability (Offences) Act in 1955 to punish practices prohibited by Article 17 of the Constitution. It was strengthened and renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act in 1976.

The constitutional ban came before this enforcement law. Neither should be confused with evidence that caste discrimination had ended. Later legislation addressed atrocities against Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
The State Bank of India is created
On 1 July 1955, the Imperial Bank of India became the State Bank of India, a state-owned institution.

Public ownership in Indian banking did not begin with the nationalisation of 14 banks in 1969. SBI was an earlier institutional step. Ownership, branch reach and actual access to useful financial services remain different questions.
AIIMS combines medical teaching, research and care

AIIMS in New Delhi was created in 1956 through an Act of Parliament as an autonomous institution of national importance. Its mandate linked medical education and training with research and health care.

A specialist teaching institution and a nationwide system of accessible primary care perform different roles. AIIMS’s establishment should be read alongside later efforts to strengthen rural health services, rather than as a substitute for them.
Inheritance law changes, with inequalities still remaining
The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 codified inheritance rules for the people to whom it applied. Daughters were included among Class I heirs, and the Act addressed women’s property rights.

The 1956 framework did not give daughters the same position as sons in Mitakshara coparcenary property. That distinction matters when reading the 2005 amendment. These were changes within a particular succession-law framework, not a single inheritance code for every Indian.
The States Reorganisation Act reorganised state boundaries substantially along linguistic lines. Demands for language-based states had already produced Andhra State in 1953.
Reorganisation accommodated regional identities within the Union. It did not settle every boundary dispute, and further states were created in later decades.
Indian military action ended Portuguese rule in Goa, Daman and Diu in December 1961. Goa commemorates its liberation on 19 December.
The end of British rule in 1947 had not ended every colonial presence in the subcontinent. Goa was initially administered within a Union Territory and attained statehood in 1987.
War with China tests the early vision
The Sino-Indian War exposed serious weaknesses in India's defence preparedness and strained the assumptions behind relations with China.
The conflict pushed defence and border security higher on the national agenda. Non-alignment did not remove the need for military capability.

eras.title: Wars, Food Security & Social Transition
eras.question: What does security mean when food is scarce?
eras.intro: Leadership changed after Nehru's death in 1964. War, drought and food shortages put immediate pressure on the state. Agricultural technology, public procurement and bank nationalisation changed how government sought to deliver security and development.
eras.tension: Higher output did not mean equal gains. Access to irrigation, credit and markets shaped who benefited from agricultural change.
events: A public institution for grain procurement and distribution

The Food Corporation of India was established in 1965 under the Food Corporations Act, 1964, against a background of grain shortages. Its functions included price-support operations, grain movement and stocks for food security.

Food security depended on more than higher-yielding seeds. Procurement, storage, transport and distribution connected farm output with public policy. FCI’s creation should be distinguished from the later 2013 statutory framework for household entitlements.
War and the call for food security
India and Pakistan fought their second war in 1965. Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri's Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan linked the soldier and the farmer.
Military security and food supply became closely connected national priorities. The Tashkent agreement followed in January 1966.
High-yielding seeds, irrigation, fertiliser and procurement support raised grain output, especially wheat. M. S. Swaminathan was a key scientific leader among many contributors.
Gains were uneven across crops, regions and farm sizes. Food security improved over time, rather than arriving immediately with the introduction of new seeds.
Congress loses ground in the states
The 1967 elections weakened Congress dominance and brought non-Congress governments to several states.
Opposition coordination and regional politics grew in importance well before the coalition governments of the 1990s.
National education policy develops across decades
The National Policy on Education of 1968 set out a framework for educational development. A new policy followed in 1986 and was modified in 1992.

Education policy therefore had a long history before NEP 2020. A policy document, a constitutional right and an enforceable statutory entitlement are different instruments. The later Right to Education framework should not be treated as another name for these earlier policies.
Indira Gandhi's government nationalised 14 major commercial banks. Six more were nationalised in 1980.
The state used banking to pursue wider access to credit and rural branches. Nationalisation was an institutional change, not proof that every lending objective was achieved.
The Indian Space Research Organisation was formed on 15 August 1969, succeeding INCOSPAR, which had been established in 1962.
Later lunar and planetary missions grew from institutions built over decades. Early ambitions included applying space technology to development, rather than concentrating only on exploration.
NDDB launched Operation Flood in 1970. Under Verghese Kurien's leadership, dairy cooperatives connected producers with urban markets.
The programme ran in phases through 1996. The White Revolution was a distinct dairy transformation, not part of the Green Revolution's grain technology package.
War and the creation of Bangladesh
The liberation struggle in East Pakistan, repression and a major refugee influx preceded the December India–Pakistan war. Pakistan's forces in the east surrendered on 16 December.
Bangladesh emerged as an independent country. Its liberation involved Bangladeshi resistance and Indian military intervention, rather than a war fought by India alone.
The Simla Agreement follows the war

India and Pakistan signed the Simla Agreement on 2 July 1972. They committed to peaceful settlement through bilateral negotiations or other mutually agreed means and to respecting the Line of Control in Jammu and Kashmir.
The agreement followed the 1971 war. It established a diplomatic framework but did not settle the Kashmir dispute or convert the Line of Control into an agreed international border.
A national framework for wildlife protection
The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 created a legal framework covering wildlife protection, regulated hunting and protected areas.

The legislation and the practical work of protecting habitats are separate parts of conservation. Later amendments changed the framework. This entry describes its 1972 origins rather than treating today’s amended law as identical to the original.
Project Tiger launched in April 1973 to conserve tigers and their habitats. It became a major national conservation programme.

A species-focused programme and a broader wildlife law are different instruments. Evaluating results requires evidence on populations, habitat connectivity, management and the experiences of communities living near protected areas. A programme’s launch does not itself establish those outcomes.
Limits on the power to amend
In Kesavananda Bharati, the Supreme Court held that Parliament's power to amend the Constitution did not extend to destroying its basic structure.
The decision became a central reference point in disputes over the relationship between Parliament, government and the courts.
The first nuclear test at Pokhran
India conducted its first underground nuclear test on 18 May 1974, commonly called Smiling Buddha. The government described it as a peaceful nuclear explosion.
It demonstrated nuclear explosive capability. The 1998 tests were a later milestone in India's declared nuclear posture.
Aryabhata, India’s first satellite, launched on 19 April 1975. It was designed and fabricated in India and carried into orbit by a Soviet Kosmos-3M rocket from Kapustin Yar.

Building a satellite and independently launching one are different technical achievements. Aryabhata demonstrated Indian spacecraft development while relying on international launch cooperation. That distinction matters when tracing the later space programme.
Sikkim became India’s 22nd state on 16 May 1975 through the constitutional transition associated with the 36th Amendment.

This was a later change in the Union, distinct from the accession and integration of princely states around independence. Statehood also requires attention to the region’s own political history, rather than treating the national map as fixed in 1947.

eras.title: Political Turmoil & the Coalition Turn
eras.question: How resilient are democratic institutions?
eras.intro: The Emergency placed extraordinary power in the executive. Its end brought an electoral transfer of power, but the following years also saw political violence, regional conflict and new demands for representation. Telecom research advanced as national politics became more fragmented.
eras.tension: National politics was changing alongside regional demands and struggles over caste representation. Electoral competition did not remove the need to protect civil liberties, minority rights and access to justice.
events: A national Emergency was proclaimed on 25 June 1975 under Indira Gandhi. Opposition leaders were detained and the press faced censorship.
Coercive sterilisation and demolitions became enduring symbols of abuse. This internal Emergency must be distinguished from earlier emergencies declared over external threats.

Enacted during the Emergency, the 42nd Amendment added Socialist and Secular to the Preamble, introduced Fundamental Duties and inserted environmental provisions, alongside wider institutional changes.

Its changes included attempts to restrict judicial review. The amendment belongs within the history of concentrated executive power as well as social and environmental provisions. Read it alongside the post-Emergency constitutional changes, including the 44th Amendment.
The Janata Party won the general election, and Morarji Desai led the first non-Congress government at the Union level.
The result demonstrated the force of electoral accountability. Internal divisions later weakened Janata, and Congress returned to power in 1980.
The 44th Amendment introduced safeguards against another internal Emergency, including replacing internal disturbance with armed rebellion as a constitutional ground.
It also protected enforcement of the rights under Articles 20 and 21 from suspension through Article 359. Legal safeguards were one response to the experience of 1975–1977.
NABARD takes on rural development finance
NABARD came into existence on 12 July 1982, taking over agricultural credit functions from the RBI and refinance functions from the Agricultural Refinance and Development Corporation.

The institution formed part of a longer effort to finance agriculture and rural development. It should not be confused with a retail bank opening an account for every farmer or with a direct cash-transfer scheme.
India wins its first cricket World Cup
Kapil Dev's team defeated the West Indies at Lord's on 25 June 1983 to win India's first men's Cricket World Cup.
The victory became a lasting sporting landmark. It should not be treated as the sole cause of cricket's later commercial and broadcasting expansion.
The Army entered the Golden Temple complex in Amritsar during Operation Blue Star, targeting armed militants.
The operation caused casualties and damage to the Akal Takht and deepened a traumatic conflict. Religious significance and civilian experiences are essential to understanding its impact.
The Centre for Development of Telematics was established in August 1984 to develop Indian telecom technology.
Its work on digital switching and rural exchanges formed part of a longer technology story. Telecom expansion preceded smartphones, UPI and the Digital India programme.
Indira Gandhi was assassinated on 31 October by two Sikh bodyguards. Anti-Sikh killings followed in Delhi and other places.
Describing these events only as riots obscures targeted violence against Sikhs. Accountability and justice remained major public issues long afterwards.
Bhopal exposes the human cost of industrial failure
A release of methyl isocyanate from the Union Carbide India pesticide plant during the night of 2–3 December caused mass deaths and injuries in Bhopal.

The disaster raises questions about industrial safety, emergency preparedness and corporate accountability. Death estimates differ by source and time period. A single number should not be presented without explaining what it counts.
The 52nd Constitutional Amendment introduced the Tenth Schedule in 1985, providing for disqualification on specified grounds of political defection by legislators.

The framework sought to address party-switching, but also raised questions about party discipline and legislators’ independence. Its original text and later amendments must be distinguished. A change in party affiliation and a legally determined disqualification are not automatically the same event.
The Assam Accord addresses a regional movement
The Union and Assam governments signed the Assam Accord on 15 August with the All Assam Students’ Union and All Assam Gana Sangram Parishad after years of agitation.

The agreement addressed migration, safeguards for Assamese identity and economic development. Its text differentiated arrivals before 1966, during 1966–1971 and on or after 25 March 1971. Signing the Accord and implementing its provisions were separate processes.
Environmental protection gains an umbrella law
The Environment (Protection) Act was enacted on 23 May 1986. It provided a broad framework for Union government action to protect and improve the environment.

It followed earlier legislation on specific environmental subjects and the 1984 Bhopal disaster. The chronological connection should not be reduced to a claim that one event alone produced the law. Enforcement, monitoring and remedies require their own assessment.
The Mizoram Accord creates a route to peace

The Mizoram Memorandum of Settlement was signed on 30 June 1986 by MNF leader Laldenga, Union Home Secretary R. D. Pradhan and Mizoram Chief Secretary Lalkhama. It followed years of insurgency and negotiations.

The settlement offered a constitutional and political route out of armed conflict. It should be studied on its own terms, alongside other regional agreements. Different movements had different demands, histories and outcomes.
Securities regulation gains an institutional base
SEBI was constituted as a non-statutory body on 12 April 1988. It became a statutory body in 1992, with its Act taking effect from 30 January that year.

The regulator’s stated remit covers investor protection and securities-market development and regulation. Its administrative creation, statutory powers and subsequent enforcement record are separate parts of the history. The transition crosses the boundary between two eras.
The voting age falls from 21 to 18
The 61st Constitutional Amendment lowered the voting age for Lok Sabha and state assembly elections from 21 to 18. Parliament passed the amendment in 1988, and it took effect in March 1989.

The first general election had used a voting age of 21. The later reduction brought younger adults into the electorate. Eligibility to vote, registration and turnout are distinct stages of electoral participation.
A specific law against caste atrocities

The Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act was enacted in 1989 and came into force on 30 January 1990. It provided for specified offences, special courts and relief and rehabilitation.

This framework extended beyond the 1955 law against untouchability. Its existence recognised the need for specific protections. Assessing enforcement requires evidence on reporting, investigation, trials and support for victims.
After the 1989 election, V. P. Singh formed a National Front government supported from outside by the BJP and Left parties.
Regional parties and negotiated parliamentary support became central to national government. Coalition politics had earlier precedents, including Janata.
Mandal brings representation to the centre
The V. P. Singh government announced implementation of the Mandal Commission's recommendation for OBC reservation in central government employment.
Support and opposition reshaped national politics around caste, representation and social justice. The policy's legal development continued through later court decisions.

eras.title: Economic Liberalisation & Globalisation
eras.question: What changes when an economy opens up?
eras.intro: A balance-of-payments crisis forced urgent decisions in 1991. Reforms reduced industrial licensing and opened more space for trade, private investment and competition. Coalition governments continued the broad shift while security crises and communal conflict challenged the country.
eras.tension: Reform was a process across several governments. The expression LPG is useful shorthand, but it hides differences between liberalisation, privatisation and global integration.
events: Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh led reforms during a severe foreign-exchange crisis. Industrial delicensing, trade changes and financial-sector reforms followed.
The shift had roots in earlier policy changes. It did not abolish all licences, remove the public sector or produce equal outcomes across regions and workers.
The Babri Masjid was demolished on 6 December 1992. Communal violence followed.
The event had lasting effects on politics, law and religious relations. Later legal decisions and the construction of the Ram temple belong to the continuing history, not to the 1992 event itself.
The 73rd and 74th Amendments were passed in 1992 and came into force in 1993, strengthening the constitutional framework for panchayats and municipalities.
They did not invent local government. They gave it a stronger constitutional basis, with elections and reservation provisions. Actual devolution still depended on state action.
Telecom policy opens space for private investment

The National Telecom Policy of 1994 sought private investment alongside the Department of Telecommunications. The 1999 policy revisited the framework after slower-than-expected private entry and financial difficulties for operators.

Later mobile and internet growth followed policy changes across several governments. The 1999 document itself acknowledged that some earlier targets remained unmet. A policy target is not evidence of a completed rollout.
Judicial review limits the use of President’s Rule
In S. R. Bommai v. Union of India, decided on 11 March 1994, the Supreme Court held that proclamations under Article 356 were subject to judicial review.

The judgment became a major reference point for the protection of federalism and state governments. It did not abolish President’s Rule. The legal justification for a proclamation and a political disagreement with a state government are different questions.
India joins the World Trade Organization
India became a WTO member on 1 January 1995. Its participation in the earlier GATT system dated to 8 July 1948.

The milestone placed India within the new multilateral trade organisation. It was not India’s first engagement with international trade rules. Membership, domestic economic reform and the distribution of trade’s benefits are related but distinct subjects.
Public internet services launched in India on 15 August 1995. The launch preceded the later spread of private internet providers, broadband and mobile data.

This was a public-service milestone, not the first use of computer networks in India. Access at launch should not be confused with widespread household connectivity. The transition to mass use took many more years.
India conducted nuclear tests on 11 and 13 May under Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee. Pakistan conducted its own tests later that month.
India openly asserted nuclear weapons capability. This did not make India a recognised nuclear-weapon State under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, which uses a different legal definition.
A national highway network takes shape
The National Highways Development Project and Golden Quadrilateral became major infrastructure priorities under the Vajpayee government.
The four-city highway network was built in stages across subsequent years. Announcement, construction and completion were separate milestones.
Indian forces fought to recover positions occupied by infiltrating Pakistani forces on the Indian side of the Line of Control in the Kargil sector.
The conflict followed the 1998 nuclear tests and the 1999 Lahore diplomatic initiative. Nuclear capability did not prevent limited conventional conflict.
Software exports and IT-enabled services expanded as Indian firms served overseas clients. Skills, telecom links and policy changes helped the sector grow.
The industry offered a new route into global markets. Its growth was concentrated in particular cities and occupations, rather than representing every part of the economy.
Three new states redraw the Union

Chhattisgarh was formed on 1 November, Uttaranchal on 9 November and Jharkhand on 15 November 2000. They were carved out of Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar respectively. Uttaranchal was later renamed Uttarakhand.

State reorganisation continued long after the linguistic changes of 1956. These movements also raised questions of regional identity, representation and development. Creating a state and improving public outcomes within it are separate historical questions.
Rural roads become a national programme
Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana launched on 25 December 2000 to improve rural road connectivity, including all-weather access for eligible unconnected habitations.

This was a different infrastructure task from widening highways between major cities. A completed road, its maintenance and its effect on access to schools, health care and markets each require separate assessment.
Gujarat violence and the demand for justice

The burning of a train at Godhra on 27 February 2002 was followed by large-scale communal violence in Gujarat. The National Human Rights Commission examined protection, relief, investigation and accountability.

The NHRC later sought Supreme Court intervention in the Best Bakery case, including an independent investigation and a retrial outside Gujarat. Its concerns illustrate why witness protection and credible trials form part of the history, alongside the violence itself.

eras.title: Economic Expansion & Rights-Based Governance
eras.question: How does growth become an entitlement?
eras.intro: The UPA governments led by Manmohan Singh combined economic expansion with legislation on information, employment and welfare. Space missions and nuclear diplomacy expanded international engagement. Terror attacks, the global financial crisis and corruption controversies tested institutions.
eras.tension: Passing a law and delivering its promise are different things. Implementation, public accountability and access shaped the reach of new entitlements.
events: The Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami of 26 December 2004 devastated coastal communities, including in India. It exposed gaps in the region’s warning and preparedness systems.

India subsequently established its tsunami early-warning centre at INCOIS, operational from October 2007. Detecting a hazard, communicating warnings and enabling communities to act are separate parts of preparedness. A warning system does not eliminate the underlying risk.
A mission to strengthen rural public health

The National Rural Health Mission launched on 12 April 2005 to improve accessible, affordable health care in rural areas. In 2013 it became one of the two sub-missions within the National Health Mission, alongside the urban mission.

Strengthening local health services is a different policy task from financing hospital treatment. Both matter to access. Announced coverage and institutional design do not, by themselves, establish service quality in every district.
The right to ask the state for information
The Right to Information Act created a national framework for access to information held by public authorities, subject to specified exemptions.
It gave citizens a route to seek records and challenge refusals. Transparency depended on functioning information commissions, record keeping and enforcement.
Rural employment becomes a legal guarantee

The employment guarantee law was enacted in 2005 and began rolling out in 2006. It guarantees at least 100 days of unskilled manual work per financial year to a rural household whose adult members volunteer for it.
The entitlement is per household, not per individual. The original NREGA name was changed to MGNREGA in 2009.

The Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act came into force on 9 September 2005. Under the amended Section 6, daughters of coparceners became coparceners by birth with the same rights and liabilities as sons in the relevant Mitakshara joint-family property.

The reform should not be described as the first time daughters could inherit under the 1956 Act. Its specific significance lay in changing coparcenary rights. Individual disputes also depended on the legislation’s terms and later judicial interpretation.
Disaster management gains a national legal framework
The Disaster Management Act was enacted on 23 December 2005. Its original framework provided for national, state and district authorities, planning and coordination for disaster management.

The Act’s enactment and the later operational development of institutions were different steps. This entry describes the 2005 framework, not every later amendment. Disaster governance also includes prevention, preparedness and recovery, beyond emergency relief alone.
Forest dwellers’ rights receive statutory recognition
The Forest Rights Act, 2006 provided for recognition of rights of forest-dwelling Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers whose rights had not been adequately recorded.

The framework included individual and community rights and processes for recognising them. Conservation policy and the rights of forest communities therefore need to be read together. Enacting the law and recognising a particular claim were different steps.
India and the United States signed their civil nuclear cooperation agreement on 10 October 2008, following years of negotiation and an NSG waiver.
It widened the scope for international civilian nuclear cooperation. It did not confer NPT nuclear-weapon State status or resolve every commercial and liability issue.
Chandrayaan-1 launched on 22 October 2008. Findings announced in 2009 included evidence of water and hydroxyl on the lunar surface from NASA's Moon Mineralogy Mapper aboard the mission.
The discovery combined an Indian mission with international instruments. The launch year and the scientific announcement year should be kept separate.
Coordinated terrorist attacks in Mumbai began on 26 November and continued for several days, striking hotels, a railway station and other locations.

The attacks prompted security changes, including the establishment of the National Investigation Agency and attention to coastal security. These changes require separate evaluation of their implementation.
Elementary education becomes an enforceable right

The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act was enacted in 2009 and came into force on 1 April 2010. It provided a legal framework for free and compulsory elementary education for children aged 6–14.
The law followed the 86th Constitutional Amendment of 2002, which inserted Article 21A. Legal entitlement, school attendance and learning outcomes are different measures of progress.
Aadhaar moves from institution to enrolment
UIDAI was established in 2009. The first Aadhaar number was issued on 29 September 2010.
Aadhaar later became part of welfare and digital service delivery. Identity infrastructure also raised questions about privacy, authentication failures and exclusion. It is not proof of citizenship.
A specialised tribunal for environmental disputes
The National Green Tribunal was established on 18 October 2010 under its 2010 Act to hear specified environmental cases and claims for relief and compensation.

The Tribunal’s establishment followed earlier environmental laws and debates over access to justice. It was not given unlimited jurisdiction over every environmental question. The creation of a forum, the orders it issues and compliance with those orders are distinct measures.
Civil society campaigns, including Anna Hazare's movement, pressed for stronger anti-corruption institutions and a Lokpal law.
The protests became a major political force. Parliament passed the Lokpal and Lokayuktas legislation in 2013. It received presidential assent in January 2014, with implementation unfolding later.
The government launched Direct Benefit Transfer on 1 January 2013 to reform delivery processes using information and communication technology. Rollout and scheme coverage expanded over time.

DBT preceded Jan Dhan’s 2014 launch and UPI’s 2016 pilot. They perform different functions: delivery of benefits, access to banking and interoperable payments. Their later combination should not erase their separate origins or the need to assess failed and delayed payments.
Food security gains a statutory framework

The National Food Security Act, 2013 established food and nutritional entitlements, including foodgrain coverage for up to 75% of the rural population and 50% of the urban population under the targeted public distribution system.

These are statutory coverage proportions, not poverty rates. Grain production, household access and nutritional outcomes measure different things. The 2013 framework built on an older public distribution system rather than creating food distribution from nothing.
Mangalyaan travels from launch to Mars
The Mars Orbiter Mission launched on 5 November 2013 and entered Mars orbit on 24 September 2014.
These milestones span a change of government. The mission is best understood as an institutional achievement across years of scientific work.
A public-health campaign reaches a major milestone
India’s last reported case of wild poliovirus occurred in Howrah on 13 January 2011. On 27 March 2014, the WHO South-East Asia Region, including India, was certified polio-free.

The result followed sustained vaccination, surveillance and work by public-health staff and partner organisations across many years. Regional certification was not a declaration of worldwide eradication, and it did not remove the need to vaccinate and monitor for poliovirus.

eras.title: Digital Transformation & Modern Geopolitics
eras.question: What does transformation look like in daily life?
eras.intro: Digital payments, tax reform and infrastructure have changed how citizens and businesses interact with the state and the economy. These years also brought the pandemic, constitutional changes in Jammu and Kashmir, and prominent space and diplomatic milestones.
eras.tension: The present is unfinished history. A programme’s launch is evidence of policy intent. Its effect on jobs, public welfare or the environment needs separate evidence over time. Selected dated coverage here reaches January 2026.
events: Jan Dhan makes financial inclusion a national mission
Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana launched on 28 August 2014 with a drive to extend banking access to unbanked households.

The programme followed earlier banking and inclusion initiatives. Opening an account is a measurable step, but regular use, access to withdrawals and successful receipt of benefits are different outcomes. The number of accounts should not automatically be treated as the number of newly banked people.
Make in India launched on 25 September 2014 to encourage investment and manufacturing.
It belongs at the start of this period, rather than being described as a new 2024 initiative. Programme goals and measured manufacturing outcomes are different claims.
UPI connects bank accounts in real time
NPCI's Unified Payments Interface had its pilot launch on 11 April 2016, before demonetisation. It enabled instant payments across participating banks.
UPI built on an existing banking and payments system. Its later adoption should not be reduced to a single policy or a single political term.
A new framework for insolvency resolution

The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code was enacted on 28 May 2016. It created a consolidated legal framework for insolvency resolution and related processes, with provisions brought into force through notifications.

Enactment did not make every part of the framework operational on the same day. Assessing its results requires distinguishing resolutions from liquidations and examining recovery, delay and the value of the assets involved. This entry describes the 2016 milestone, rather than every later amendment.
On 8 November, the government announced withdrawal of the legal-tender status of existing ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes, subject to specified exceptions and exchange arrangements.
The policy caused a major cash disruption. Claims about lasting effects on black money, counterfeiting, formalisation or digital adoption require evidence beyond the announcement itself.
Disability law broadens its rights framework

The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 replaced the earlier 1995 legislation and expanded the recognised disability categories from seven to twenty-one. It addressed rights and duties across areas including education, employment and accessibility.

The legislation represented a broader framework, rather than proof that physical, digital and social barriers had disappeared. Some provisions distinguish persons with disabilities from persons with benchmark disabilities. The categories should not be treated as interchangeable.
Goods and Services Tax rolled out on 1 July 2017 following a constitutional amendment and negotiation between the Union and states.
GST subsumed many indirect taxes through a dual Union–state framework. It did not replace every indirect tax or create a single tax rate for all goods and services.
Privacy is recognised as a fundamental right
On 24 August 2017, a nine-judge Supreme Court bench recognised the constitutional protection of privacy in the Puttaswamy case.

The decision gave constitutional weight to questions about personal information, dignity and state power. It should be distinguished from the separate Aadhaar judgment in 2018 and from later legislation on data protection.
The Supreme Court reads down Section 377
On 6 September 2018, the Supreme Court in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India held Section 377 unconstitutional insofar as it criminalised consensual sexual conduct between adults of the same sex.

The decision addressed criminalisation and constitutional protections of dignity, liberty and equality. It should not be described as a judgment that established same-sex marriage. Legal reform and the lived experience of discrimination remain distinct subjects.
PM-JAY adds publicly financed hospital cover
Ayushman Bharat–Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana launched on 23 September 2018 in Ranchi. Its design provided health cover for eligible families for specified secondary and tertiary hospital care.

Hospital treatment cover is not the same as universal access to every kind of health care. Primary care, outpatient costs, provider availability and treatment quality require separate attention. This entry describes the launch; later eligibility expansions are separate milestones.
August constitutional measures rendered Article 370's special-status provisions inoperative. Reorganisation took effect on 31 October, creating the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh.
The August constitutional change and October administrative reorganisation were distinct steps. Their effects on rights, representation and security require attention beyond the legal announcements.
COVID-19 brought lockdowns, migration distress and severe pressure on health services. India began its national vaccination programme on 16 January 2021.

Covaxin was developed in India. Covishield was manufactured in India from the Oxford–AstraZeneca vaccine. Vaccine Maitri involved overseas supplies and was distinct from the domestic vaccination campaign.
PLI programmes expanded across 14 manufacturing sectors, with a ₹1.97 lakh crore outlay announced in the 2021–22 Union Budget.

Incentive commitments are not the same as realised investment, employment or domestic value addition. Those outcomes need sector-specific assessment. Energy transition also remains an ongoing policy area.
NEP 2020 sets out a new education framework

The Union Cabinet approved National Education Policy 2020 on 29 July. It proposed changes across school and higher education, including a 5+3+3+4 curricular and pedagogical structure that included early childhood education.

The proposal followed earlier national policies and a multi-year consultation process. Cabinet approval did not mean that every institution changed immediately. Implementation depended on subsequent decisions and action across governments and educational bodies.

Parliament passed three farm laws in September 2020. Following sustained farmer protests, Parliament passed repeal legislation in November 2021. The Farm Laws Repeal Act received assent on 30 November.

The repeal reversed those legislative changes. It did not, by itself, resolve wider disputes over agricultural markets, procurement or minimum support prices. Policy design and the process of building public consent are both part of this history.
The National Green Hydrogen Mission set out a framework for developing production, demand and infrastructure for green hydrogen.
It is one part of a wider energy transition. Announced targets describe intended outcomes, rather than hydrogen already produced or emissions already avoided.
A soft landing in the Moon's southern high latitudes
Chandrayaan-3 successfully soft-landed on 23 August 2023. India became the fourth country to achieve a lunar soft landing.
The landing site was around 69° south latitude. It was in the southern high-latitude region, not at the geographic south pole itself.
The New Delhi summit on 9–10 September adopted a leaders' declaration. The African Union joined the G20 as a permanent member.
The declaration recorded negotiated commitments on development and international cooperation. Summit agreements and their later implementation should be assessed separately.
The BJP won 240 Lok Sabha seats and Congress 99. The BJP fell short of a majority on its own, and an NDA coalition returned to government under Narendra Modi.
The result differed from the BJP's single-party majorities in 2014 and 2019. It renewed the importance of allies within the governing coalition.
ISRO successfully docked the two SpaDeX satellites on 16 January 2025.
The experiment demonstrated a capability relevant to future missions requiring spacecraft to meet and connect in orbit. It did not itself constitute an operational Indian space station.
NISAR adds a joint Earth-observation mission
The joint NASA–ISRO NISAR mission launched on 30 July 2025 aboard GSLV-F16.
The mission extends the space story beyond lunar exploration to observing the Earth. Its joint development also illustrates the continuing role of international scientific cooperation.
WHO records fifteen years without a regional wild-polio case
On 13 January 2026, WHO reported that its South-East Asia Region had sustained its polio-free status fifteen years after the last wild-poliovirus case, recorded in India in 2011.

This is a dated regional status report that includes India, rather than a claim of global eradication. WHO emphasised continued vaccination and surveillance against importation. Sustaining an achievement is a separate public-health task from reaching certification.
